column4: The section defines taqwa as protection from what is feared; this ayah says God protects the righteous from the evil of that Day, making the protective result explicit.
The section describes taqwa as putting oneself under a shield from danger; here their Lord protects them from the punishment of Hell.
In Pharaoh’s setting, God protects the believing man from the evils of the plot against him; this gives the section’s protective sense of taqwa a concrete human danger.
This ayah says that whoever is spared the punishment of that Day has received mercy, a direct instance of the section’s protection from what is feared.

The root of taqwa also describes precaution against danger from hostile people; this ayah allows such protection as an exception to taking them as allies, making the protective boundary social and concrete.
The section sets taqwa between the self and harm; this ayah says that fearing God brings a criterion that distinguishes right from wrong, extending protection into discernment.
Pharaoh’s claim to be the highest lord is a specific expression of the transgression named for him in 79:17 and in the section’s discussion of crossing the limit.
This ayah says God seized Pharaoh as a chastening example; it supplies the consequence of the claim in 79:24 and the transgression named in 79:17.
The next ayah says Pharaoh’s fate is a lesson for the one who fears; it makes the section’s warning to restrain oneself through fear an explicit audience for this example.

Water runs through valleys in measured amounts, and a flood carries foam that disappears while what benefits people remains; this gives the section’s burst-and-barrier image a specific contrast between transient excess and lasting benefit.
In Noah’s flood, the oven’s gushing is the sign that the flood has begun; it supplies a second Quranic scene of water bursting forth before the ark carries those protected from it.
Noah’s ship runs through waves like mountains; this is a direct picture of the flood’s scale in the section’s physical-water image.

Noah’s son trusts a mountain to protect him from the water, but a wave separates and drowns him; his failed refuge contrasts with the ark’s protection in 11:42 and the section’s shield against danger.
This retelling pairs the oven’s gushing with the command to load the ark; it is another specific account of bursting floodwater and the refuge prepared against it.

People describe Gog and Magog as corruptors on earth and ask Dhul-Qarnayn to build a barrier between them and the people; this directly stages protection placed between a feared force and those it threatens.
Dhul-Qarnayn accepts the task of making a barrier; this supplies his answer to the request in 18:94 and turns the section’s protective boundary into a built one.
This ayah describes the iron and molten-copper construction of the barrier requested in 18:94, making the act of setting a firm boundary concrete.
Gog and Magog cannot climb over or pierce the completed barrier; its own contribution is the protection that keeps the corrupters from crossing into the people’s space.
Dhul-Qarnayn says the barrier is a mercy but will be leveled when God’s promise comes; this marks the protection as a boundary that will eventually be removed.
Once that barrier is removed, people surge against one another; this is the section’s image of an unchecked flow made social and visible.
The release of Gog and Magog sends them rushing down from every height; it repeats the section’s image of transgression breaking outward once restraint is gone.

This continuation explains the harmful movement withheld in 9:46: if those people had set out, they would have rushed among the community spreading confusion and sedition, a specific case of bad movement spreading to others.

The section warns against following the musrifin, those who exceed limits; this ayah describes God’s servants as neither extravagant nor miserly in spending, giving a concrete picture of the restraint between excess and deficiency.
This ayah commands people to eat and drink without excess; it repeats the section’s warning against the musrifin as a limit on consumption.
The command not to obey a person who follows desire and exceeds bounds parallels Salih’s warning not to follow the musrifin, making the danger of following an unrestrained leader specific.

The section presents fujur as releasing the self into disobedience; this ayah says that if truth followed people’s desires, the heavens and earth would be corrupted, showing the scale of disorder that unchecked desire would produce.
Qarun is told not to seek corruption in the land; this echoes Salih’s specific command not to follow those who spread corruption and makes restraint an answer to transgression.
Qarun claims his wealth came from his own knowledge, a concrete form of the self-sufficiency that the section links to human transgression and that 96:7 names as its trigger.
The earth swallows Qarun and his dwelling after his boast; the land itself takes the overreaching person down, a specific reversal of the section’s image of overflow returning upon its source.
On the Day of Judgment a wall separates the believers from the hypocrites, with mercy on one side and punishment on the other; it gives the section’s protective boundary a specific moral division.
